title: The dot product: how much lies along

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is a's shadow on b's line shrinking to a dot at 90°, then falling behind the start as the dot product turns negative, when you swing a round.
interactive.title: The shadow on the line
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: Two arrows, a and b, start from one point on a grid. You can drag either tip. A light shines onto b's line, square to it. So a casts a shadow along that line. The shadow's length is the part of a that lies along b. It is |a| cos θ, where θ is the angle between the arrows. Multiply the shadow by b's length and you get the dot product, a·b. Two readouts work it out in two ways, and they always agree. One is |a||b| cos θ. The other adds up the parts, a₁b₁ + a₂b₂, with + a₃b₃ in 3-D. At 90° the shadow shrinks to a dot. Past 90° it falls behind the start and counts as minus. The screens run like this. First come a = 3i + 4j and b = 4i. The shadow is 3 and the dot product is 12. A puzzle asks for a·b with b = 6i. Next, a swings round from 0°. It rests at 90°, then goes on to 135°. A puzzle gives sizes 5 and 4 at 120°. Then the parts pair up, because i·i = 1 and i·j = 0. A puzzle asks which arrow is square to 2i + 1j. Then comes the angle between two arrows in 3-D. You can drag that picture sideways to turn it. A puzzle finds the angle between 2i + 2j + 1k and 2i − 1j + 2k. Then the arrows become a rope and a rail. Only the pull along the rail does work. A puzzle has a rope pulling 150i + 200j N. Two mixed puzzles come last. In one, the arrows are a voltage and a current. In the other, a rope pulls back against a sliding crate. Some screens show an idea. The rest ask you to try it. Each puzzle offers three answers. A wrong pick is drawn too, so you can see where it goes wrong.
interactive.ignores: The light shines square onto b's line. A real sun's shadow slants. Its length also changes with the time of day. The rope's pull is held steady. The trolley runs on a straight rail with no friction. A pull that changes along a curved path needs the dot product added up bit by bit. That waits for Vector calculus. The voltage and current are drawn as arrows. But their angle is a shift in time, not a direction in space. The puzzles use example values, rounded to two decimal places.

explain.text:
The dot product of two vectors is a plain number. It says how much of one lies along the other, times the other's length.

Draw a and b from one point. Shine a light onto b's line, square to it. The shadow of a falls along that line. Its length is |a| cos θ, where θ is the angle between them. Cos picks out the side next to the angle, just as it does when you resolve. Multiply the shadow by b's length and you have the [[dot product]], a·b = |a||b| cos θ.[^1] It is also called the scalar product. Take a = 3i + 4j and b = 4i. The shadow is 3 long. So a·b = 3 × 4 = 12. Multiplying the sizes gives 5 × 4 = 20. That counts the whole of a, but only the part along b should count. Sin gives the part square to b. That part casts no shadow on b's line. A shadow is a length, not an arrow. So the dot product is a scalar, a plain number.[^2]

As a swings round, the shadow follows cos θ. At 90° it shrinks to a dot. So a·b = 0. Past 90° the shadow falls behind the start and counts as minus.[^3] Two arrows square to each other always give 0. A positive dot product means they lean the same way. A negative one means they lean apart.

You can also work it out from the parts. The rule reads the same either way round. So b's shadow on a's line works just as well. Split b into its parts, laid nose to tail. Their shadows on a's line sit end to end. So a·b is the sum of what each part gives. Now, a·i is a's shadow on the x-axis, times 1. That is a's across part, a₁. Stretch i by b₁ and its dot product with a stretches by b₁ too. So the part b₁i gives a₁b₁. The same holds up the page and along k. That leaves a·b = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂ + a₃b₃. The axes show the same thing. The arrow i lies along itself and is 1 long. So i·i = 1 × 1 × cos 0° = 1. The arrows i and j are square to each other. So i·j = 0. For 3i + 4j and 4i + 3j, the dot product is 12 + 12 = 24. Put the two ways together and you get the angle between two arrows: cos θ = a·b ÷ (|a||b|).

Work is a dot product. A steady force F that moves something through a straight move d does work F·d.[^4] Only the part of the pull along the move counts. Take a 200 N pull at 30° to a rail, over 5 m. It does 200 × 5 × cos 30° = 866.03 J of work. True power, V I cos φ, has the same shape. It is two sizes times the cosine of the angle between them. V I on its own is the apparent power, in VA.[^5]

**The dot product is a plain number: how much of one vector lies along the other, times the other's length. Work it out as |a||b| cos θ or as a₁b₁ + a₂b₂ + a₃b₃.**

analogy.text: Think of a sloping cable run on a plan drawing. Seen from straight above, the run looks shorter than it is. Its length on the plan is its true length times cos of the slope. A flat run shows its full length. A vertical drop is just a dot. The plan length is the run's shadow. It is the part that lies along the floor.
analogy.breaks: A plan gives only the shadow's length. The dot product also multiplies it by the other arrow's length. A length on a drawing is never below zero. A dot product goes negative once the angle passes 90°.

practice.text:
- Write both vectors as i, j and k parts.
- Multiply the across parts together, then the up parts, then the k parts. Add the three results.
- Know the sizes and the angle instead? Use |a||b| cos θ. Take the angle between the two arrows drawn from one point.
- To find the angle, divide the dot product by the two sizes multiplied together. Then take cos⁻¹.
- Read the sign. Positive means the two lean the same way. Zero means they are square. Negative means they lean apart.

**Rule of thumb:** A zero dot product is the quickest test that two arrows are square. For work, only the part of the force along the move counts.

**Worked example:** A pull F = 120i + 50j N drags a load through d = 3i + 4j m. The work is 120 × 3 + 50 × 4 = 360 + 200 = 560 J. The pull's size is √(120² + 50²) = 130 N. The move's size is 5 m. So cos θ = 560 ÷ 650, about 0.86. The pull runs 30.51° off the move.

**Common mistakes**
- Giving the answer as an arrow. The dot product is a plain number. It has no i or j.
- Using sin in place of cos. The shadow is the side next to the angle.
- Losing the minus past 90°. A rope pulling back against a move does negative work.
- Multiplying the sizes and forgetting the angle. That gives the dot product only when the arrows point the same way.
- Adding the sizes when you find the angle. Divide by the sizes multiplied, not added.

sources.quote: The scalar product of two vectors is obtained by multiplying their magnitudes with the cosine of the angle between them.

sources.title: 2.4 Products of Vectors - University Physics Volume 1 | OpenStax
sources.quote: The dot product is a scalar; the cross product is a vector.

sources.title: Ch. 2 Summary - University Physics Volume 1 | OpenStax
sources.quote: The scalar product of orthogonal vectors vanishes; the scalar product of antiparallel vectors is negative.

sources.title: 2.4 Products of Vectors - University Physics Volume 1 | OpenStax
sources.quote: For example, the work that a force (a vector) performs on an object while causing its displacement (a vector) is defined as a scalar product of the force vector with the displacement vector.

sources.title: Difference Between Active Power, Reactive Power and Apparent Power – Schneider Electric
sources.quote: The apparent power of a sinusoidal AC circuit can be calculated simply as the product of its RMS values for voltage and current. It is measured in volt-amperes (VA) or kilovolt-amps (kVA).
